hints: Start by comparing the very first point in 1980 with the very last point in 2000 - is the line higher or lower overall?
Now break the 20 years into sections - look for where the line falls steeply, stays fairly flat, rises again, then falls.
Pick out actual numbers from the y-axis for 1980, the low point around 1984, the peak around 1992 and 2000 to support each trend.
walkthrough:
Get the Big Picture First**
Look at the start and end of the curve. In 1980 the value is just under 28,000, about 27,700 to 27,800 cases. In 2000 it is about 16,300 to 16,400 cases. So over the whole period there is a clear overall decrease of about 11,400 cases.

Split Into Phases**
The fall is not steady. From 1980 to 1984 there is a steep fall to about 22,100 cases. From 1984 to 1988 there is little change, a slight rise and fall around 22,000 to 22,700. Then from 1988 to 1992 there is a rise to a peak of about 26,600 to 26,700 in 1992.

Finish With Data-Supported Description**
After 1992 there is a steady decrease all the way to 2000. Good answers always quote years and numbers with the trend, for example decrease from 1980 to 1984, increase from 1988 to 1992, decrease after 1992 to 2000.

Final answer: Overall decrease in number of reported cases from approx. 27,800 in 1980 to approx. 16,300 in 2000. Sharp decrease 1980 to 1984, then increase 1984/1988 to peak approx. 26,700 in 1992, followed by decrease 1992 to 2000.

hints: Think about which cells HIV attacks and what that means for the ability to fight other pathogens like Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Think about people who already carry TB bacteria without symptoms - what happens to that latent infection if immunity fails?
walkthrough:
Link HIV to Weak Immunity**
HIV infects and destroys T-helper lymphocytes. That weakens both cell-mediated and humoral responses, so the person cannot control pathogens as well. TB caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis acts as an opportunistic disease in this situation.

Link Weak Immunity to More TB Cases**
Many people carry latent TB kept in check by the immune system. When immunity falls, latent TB reactivates to active disease. More HIV infections also means more spread of TB to others, so reported TB cases rise between 1984 and 1992.
Final answer: HIV weakens the immune system, making people more susceptible to TB. Latent TB is more likely to become active TB in people living with HIV, e.g. due to fall in T-helper lymphocytes.

hints: Think about selection pressure - what prescribing habits give resistant bacteria an advantage?
Think about making sure treatment actually kills all the bacteria, plus ways to reduce the need for antibiotics at all.
walkthrough:
Reduce Selection Pressure**
Resistance spreads when antibiotics are overused. So prescribe antibiotics only when absolutely necessary and do not use them for viral infections or as preventative medicine. Reducing use in farming also helps.

Make Treatment Effective and Prevent Spread**
Use the correct effective antibiotic at the correct dose and complete the whole course, so no bacteria survive to pass on resistance. Developing new antibiotics and preventing infection by vaccination, hospital hygiene and quarantine reduces the impact of resistant strains.

Final answer: Only prescribe/use antibiotics when necessary, e.g. not for viral infections. Ensure correct antibiotic, correct dose and complete full course. Any one other: develop new antibiotics / improve hygiene, vaccination and isolation to prevent spread / reduce agricultural use.

hints: Recall what the C-shaped cartilage does in the trachea and the plates of cartilage in the bronchi during pressure changes in breathing.
walkthrough:
Remember Why Cartilage Is There**
Cartilage is stiff tissue that holds the airway open when air pressure changes during breathing in and out. If TB damages it, that support is lost, so the bronchus can collapse or narrow and air flow is reduced.
Final answer: Bronchi may collapse / lose structural support and narrow, restricting airflow.

hints: Think about where mucus and cilia are needed to trap and move particles - in the conducting airways or in the tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens?
Think about which wall needs smooth muscle to control diameter and which wall needs only a very thin surface for diffusion.
Check the pattern - three cell types belong to trachea and bronchus but not alveolus, while one cell type belongs only to the alveolus.
walkthrough:
Conducting Airways Share the Same Protection**
Trachea and bronchus both have ciliated epithelial cells to sweep mucus, goblet cells to secrete mucus, and smooth muscle cells to constrict the airway. So those three rows are cross for alveolus, tick for bronchus, tick for trachea.

Alveoli Are Built for Gas Exchange**
Alveoli need a very short diffusion distance, so their wall is thin squamous epithelium. They have no cilia, no goblet cells and no smooth muscle. So squamous epithelial cell is tick for alveolus, cross for bronchus, cross for trachea.

Complete Every Box**
Put a tick if present and a cross if not present in every box. The pattern is three ticks in the bronchus and trachea columns for the first three rows, and one tick in the alveolus column for the last row.

Final answer: ciliated epithelial cell: alveolus X, bronchus tick, trachea tick; goblet cell: alveolus X, bronchus tick, trachea tick; smooth muscle cell: alveolus X, bronchus tick, trachea tick; squamous epithelial cell: alveolus tick, bronchus X, trachea X.
